title: Strong Passwords
about: How passwords get guessed, and how to make yours hard to crack.

cards.prompt: Your friend's game account was taken over. Their password was `max2019`. A computer could guess that in seconds.
cards.explanation: True. A pet's name and a year is one of the first things a guesser tries, and a computer makes about a **billion guesses a second**.
cards.hint: How long is it, and would a guesser try a pet's name early?
cards.nudge: Short passwords made of a name and a year are guessed almost straight away.

cards.prompt: **Drag the slider** until a computer would need **100+ years** to guess this password.
cards.explanation: A computer makes about a **billion guesses a second**, and each extra letter multiplies its work by **26**. **Length** is what makes a password strong.
cards.hint: Drag the slider to the right and watch the time shoot up.
cards.nudge: Keep going: every extra letter multiplies the time by 26.

cards.sentence: A **passphrase** is four or more **random** words, like `otter planet brick soup`: never a song line or quote.

cards.prompt: Which one takes a computer **longer** to guess?

options.nudge: Symbols help a little, but it's only 8 characters. Think back to the slider.
A word plus a year is one of the first things guessed, and it's fairly short.

cards.hint: What made the time shoot up on the slider?
cards.explanation: **Length wins.** Four random words make a long password that's easy to remember: a **passphrase**. Australia's cyber experts (cyber.gov.au) recommend one.

items.label: Your pet's name and birth year
A line from a famous song

cards.explanation: Common passwords, names, birth years and song lines are **tried first**. Random words must be found by trying every combination.
cards.hint: Would a guesser try it early: a common password, a name, a year or a famous line?
cards.nudge: Look at each one again: is it on a guesser's early list, or long and random?

cards.prompt: Swapping `a` for `@` makes a password much harder to guess.
cards.explanation: False. Swaps like `P@ssw0rd` are one of the first tricks guessers try. Random words beat swaps.
cards.hint: Would a guesser think of swapping `a` for `@`?
cards.nudge: Guessers know every common swap, so they try them early.

options.nudge: Long is good, but if one site leaks it, the same password opens the rest.
Using the same one everywhere means one leak opens every account.

cards.explanation: If one site leaks a password, attackers try it everywhere. Its **own** password keeps each account safe.
cards.hint: What happens to your other accounts if one site leaks your password?

cards.prompt: Only **10 characters** allowed. Add kinds of characters to reach **100 years**.
cards.explanation: More kinds of characters means more to try, so a **short random** password can reach 100 years. But it's hard to remember, so long passphrases suit people better.
cards.hint: Each switch adds more characters a guesser has to try.
cards.nudge: Keep adding kinds of characters until the time passes 100 years.

cards.prompt: A game site was hacked, and passwords were stolen: a [[data breach]].

steps.text: You used that password for your **email** too. What first?

choices.text: Change your email password to a new one
choices.consequence: Good. Your email is the most important account: it can reset all the others.
The same password opens your email too. Attackers try stolen passwords on other sites.
The stolen password still opens your email. That's the one to change first.

steps.text: Your email is safe. And the game?

choices.text: Give it its own new password
choices.consequence: Now each account has its own password, so one leak can't open the other.

choices.text: Use the new email password too
choices.consequence: Then the next breach could open your email again. Every account needs its own password.

cards.explanation: Change a stolen password everywhere you used it, starting with your **email**, which can reset the rest. Every account needs its own password.
cards.hint: Which account could be used to reset all your others?

cards.prompt: Mia's passphrase is a line from her favourite song.

choices.text: Not really: song lines get guessed early
choices.consequence: Right. Guessers try lyrics and famous lines early. Length only helps when the words are random.
Length isn't enough on its own. A famous line is in guessing lists, so it falls early.

choices.text: Yes, if she adds ! to the end
choices.consequence: A symbol on the end is one of the first tricks guessers try. The words need to be random.
Now it's long **and** unpredictable. She can still picture the words to remember them.

choices.text: Pick an old song nobody knows
choices.consequence: Guessing lists hold huge numbers of songs, not just popular ones. The words need to be random.

cards.explanation: A passphrase needs **random** words. Lyrics and quotes are long but predictable, so guessers try them early.
cards.hint: Length is one thing that makes a passphrase strong. What's the other?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **Length** wins: a **passphrase** is four or more **random** words.
- Give every account its **own** password.
- **Try this:** change one password you reuse into a four-word passphrase.
